3.6.lead: Figure 3.6 shows why total frame count alone does not describe the supervision available to the learner. Acquisition and soda-can pickup segments last longer than deposit or radio-interaction segments, while next-action targets change much less in wait and follow than in the two manipulation contexts. Eligibility for a complete action horizon further changes the available anchor population. These descriptive differences motivate RQ1: chunk construction and sampling determine which recorded rows contribute to learning. Repeated segments within each source are correlated.

(b) Across-source distributions of the mean absolute difference between next-action targets and current states over 18 revolute torso/arm joints, with 45 sources per context. Boxes show medians and interquartile ranges; whiskers use the 10th–90th percentiles, with more extreme values omitted. (c) Recorded frames and eligible B/C anchors from actual masks; labels show valid/raw ratios. Panels (a,b) use logarithmic axes.

5.4.lead: Figure 5.4 compares the event-detection profiles in the two manipulation contexts. B20 and C20 have higher mean F1 than A20 on the frozen validation anchors, but precision remains limited: the highest pickup precision is 0.3163. Radio scores also vary substantially with inference noise. These differences do not establish successful grasping, a single-factor causal effect, or statistical significance. A20 to B20 changes prompts and sampling together; B20 to C20 changes state and action normalisation together.

Points show mean F1 and precision; bars show sample standard deviations over five inference flow-noise seeds. Each seed pools event counts over 200 matched validation anchors per context. Each checkpoint comes from one training run; the bars are not training-run uncertainty or confidence intervals. Lines guide comparison between configurations. SD bars are untruncated and may extend below zero. Higher event scores do not establish successful grasping.
